EIGHTEENTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 313
June 2, 1902.
Appointment to existing vacancy in position of assistant commissioner of immigra¬
tion at the port of New York allowed without examination.
June 21, 1902.
Alexander C. Caine, examiner in the Department of Justice, allowed to be trans¬
ferred to position of clerk of class 4 for designation as disbursing clerk in the Depart¬
ment of Justice.
July 25, 1902.
Miss Ellen W. Fitzsimons was separated from the position of clerk at $1,000 by
reason of the abolition of the office of the Commissioner of Railroads on June 30,
1902. Her reinstatement for the purpose of transfer to the Post-Office Department
was requested, and in view of the cause of her separation the President ordered that
the requirements of section 11, Rule X, be waived.
July 30, 1902.
Appointment to existing vacancy in position of clerk at $1,000 per annum in the
War Department allowed without examination, the person so appointed to be detailed
for duty at the White House.
August 12, 1902.
In a request for the reinstatement in the Government Printing Office of John T.
Heck, who had been out of the service for more than one year, the requirement of
Rule IX in regard to the year limit was waived.

III. ORDERS OF CLASSIFICATION BY PRESIDENTS, BY
HEADS OF DEPARTMENTS AND OFFICES, AND BY
CONGRESS.
In the Fourth Report of this Commission, pages 102 to 120, the history of the sev¬
eral classifications of the United States civil service is brought down to the early
part of 1888. On page 207 is given a summary of the classifications in the several
Departments and in the Customs and the Postal services.
On February 2, 1888, President Cleveland promulgated the “Amended Civil￾Service Rules,” to take effect on March 1, 1888. In a letter of March 21, discussing
some of the provisions of these rules, he said:
* * * Difficulties which now embarrass the execution of the civil-service law
would be obviated if there was a better and uniform classification of the employees
in the different departments. The importance of this is entirely obvious. The
present imperfect classifications, hastily made, apparently with but little care for
uniformity, and promulgated after the late Presidential election and prior to the
installation of the present Administration, should* not have been permitted to con¬
tinue until this time. * * * I wish the Commission would revise these classifi¬
cations and submit to me a plan which will, as far as possible, make them uniform,
and which will especially remedy the present condition which permits persons to
enter a grade in the service in the one department without any examination which
in another department can only be entered after passing such examination. This, I
think, should be done by extending the limits of the classified service rather than
by contracting them.
Accordingly, the Commission submitted a uniform classification for the Depart¬
mental Service, which was approved by the President and adopted by the several
departments on the following dates in 1888: Treasury, Navy, Post-Office, and Interior
Departments, June 29; War and Agriculture Departments, June 30; State Depart¬
ment, July 3; Department of Justice,, July 5.
The language of the classification order was as follows:
DEPARTMENTAL SERVICE.
By direction of the President of the United States, and in accordance with the third
clause of section 6 of the act entitled “An act to regulate and improve the civil serv¬
ice of the United States,” approved January 16, 1883,
It is ordered, That the officers, clerks, and other employees of this Department be,
and they are hereby, arranged in the following classes, viz:
Class A.—All persons receiving an

ORDERS AMENDING SCHEDULE A.
PAYMASTERS, NEW YORK CUSTOMS DISTRICT.
June 25, 1908.
Schedule A, Subdivision II, paragraph 4, of the civil-service rules, which at
present excepts from the requirement of examination:
In the New York customs district: One paymaster; stitch counters,
is hereby amended to read as follows:
In the New York customs district: Two paymasters; stitch counters.
The volume of business in the New York customs district had increased to
such an extent that the collector of customs at the port of New York found it
necessary to employ an additional paymaster to assist in paying the force em¬
ployed outside the collector’s office. Inasmuch as only one paymaster was
excepted under Schedule A, it was necessary to make the foregoing amendment
to permit the employment of an additional paymaster.
CIVILIAN INSTRUCTORS, U. S. MILITARY AND NAVAL ACADEMIES.
September 3, 1908.
The civil-service rules, Schedule A, Section III, War Department, is hereby
amended by adding a new paragraph, to be numbered 11, and to read as follows:
11. Civilian professors, instructors, and teachers in the U. S. Military
Academy at West Point and in the U. S. Naval Academy at Annapolis.
The academies at West Point and Annapolis are institutions of the grade of
colleges. In filling positions in colleges it is customary to look for experts, men
who have achieved success in other institutions of a similar character. The
personal equation is highly important. The number of persons who make
thoroughly successful college professors is not large and it is impossible to
handle successfully a university or college without absolute control over the
personnel of its corps of instructors. For these reasons it seemed improbable
that competent men could be secured for these positions through the ordinary
competitive examination.
INSPECTING ENGINEER AND INSPECTORS, ISTHMIAN CANAL SERVICE.
October 3, 1908.
Schedule A, Subdivision VIII, relating to the Isthmian Canal Commission, is
hereby amended as follows: The present paragraph will be numbered 1, but
will remain otherwise unchanged. A new paragraph, to be numbered 2, to read
as follows, is hereby added:
2. One inspecting engineer and inspectors in the purchasing department.
The work of inspection of supplies and materials for the Panama Canal was
for a time carried on jointly by the Panama Railroad Company and the canal
commission. In the summer of 1907 the purchasing department was placed
under the Chief of Engiheers of the War Department and the general purchas¬
ing officer of the canal commission availed himself of the services of the engi¬
neer officers of the army throughout the country. This, however, did not take

York, and in March, 1908, a portion of this force was transferred to Washing¬
ton. This force was on the railroad company’s pay roll, although the canal com¬
mission paid one-half the expenses. It became desirable to separate the inspec¬
tion work in order to obtain an accurate division of expenses and to promote the
greater efficiency of the service. An executive order was, therefore, desired,
placing the clerical force under the civil-service rules and bringing the persons
then employed into the classified service (see p. 127). It was also desired that
the inspecting engineer and the inspectors under him should be excepted from
examination owing to the character of the duties and the responsibility of the
positions.
CIVILIAN INSTRUCTORS, U. S. REVENUE-CUTTER SERVICE.
October 21, 1908.
Schedule A, Section II, of the civil-service rules, is hereby amended by the
addition of a new paragraph, to be numbered 12, and to read as follows:
12. Civilian instructors in the U. S. Revenue-Cutter Service.
The reasons favoring this amendment were similar to those advanced in
favor of similar action in the case of civilian professors, instructors, and teach¬
ers in the Military Academy and the Naval Academy, whose positions were
excepted by the executive order of September 3, 1908.

the office of the Secretary of the United States Senate from June 30, 1905, to March 31, 1909, may be reinstated in an appropriate position in the classified service. 
Mr Garver was appointed on July 3, 1904, as a forest assistant in the General Land 
Office. He was transferred by act of Congress, with his position, to the Department of 
Agriculture on February 1, 1905, from which department he resigned on June 26, 1905. 
From that date until March 31, 1909, he served as a clerk in the office of the Secretary 
of the United States Senate. Civil-service Rule X, paragraph 3, provides that any 
person may be retransferred to a position in which he was formerly employed or to any 
position to which transfer could be made therefrom if, since his transfer, he has been 
continuously in the executive or judicial civil service of the United States or of its 
insular possessions. As Mr. Garver had been serving in the legislative service the 
provisions of this rule did not permit his retransfer, but there appeared to be no reason 
why he should not logically be entitled to retransfer, and the Commission recom￾mended the issuance of the above order. 
April 7, 1909. 
Mrs. Nannie M. Wayland may be reinstated in the classified service in the Treasury Department without regard to the length of time that she has been separated from the service. 
Mrs. Wayland had formerly served as a clerk in the Treasury Department, but was 
separated by resignation on April 19, 1907. On November 27 of that year the Com￾mission authorized her reinstatement in the Treasury Department, with a view to 
her immediate transfer to the Philippine service. Mrs. Wayland was not transferred 
to the Philippine service under this authority, but did serve for a short period in the 
federal service in the Philippines. Her year of eligibility for reinstatement expired 
on April 19, 1908, and the above executive order was necessary to authorize her rein￾statement after that date. 
April 16, 1909. 
Mr. Archibald S. Pinkett, of Pennsylvania, may be appointed to a clerkship in the Department of State without examination under the civil-service act and rules. This order is made at the request and upon the recommendation of the Secretary of State, who has knowledge of Mr. Pinkett’s fitness from his clerical service under the Secretary while he was a Senator in Congress. Miss Frances M. Marsh, of Pennsylvania, may be appointed to a clerkship in the Department of State, without examination under the civil-service act and rules. This order is made at the request and upon recommendation of the Secretary of State, who has knowledge of Miss Marsh’s fitness from her clerical services under him while a Senator in Congress. 
As stated in the orders, both Mr. Pinkett and Miss Marsh had served under the 
Secretary of State while he was a Senator in Congress, and on account of his knowledge 
of their qualifications he recommended their appointments in the Department of State. 
May 17, 1909. 
Mrs. Nina L. Carrington, whose competency is certified to by those civil officers with whom she has had temporary employment, may be appointed to a clerkship in the classified service without examination for the reason that her husband, Frank Del. Carrington, late major, First U. S. Infantry, was unjustly convicted in the civil courts of the Philippines of certain criminal charges, as now decided by the Supreme Court, and this action is in the nature of a remedial measure within the power of the President to rectify the injustice of those proceedings, which have led to the very straitened and necessitous condition of Mrs. Carrington and her family. 
May 28, 19089.

In view of the exceptional qualifications of Mr. George M. Wrattan, his experience of many years as interpreter for the Apache Indians, and the improbability that a competitive examination would result in obtaining eligibles equally qualified for the position, Mr. Wrattan may be reemployed as an interpreter without regard to the fact that he has been separated from the service for more than one year. 
Mr. Wrattan had formerly served as an interpreter in the Quartermaster’s Depart￾ment at Large and was classified by the revision and extension of the rules on May 6, 
1896. He resigned from the service on February 15, 1908, and inasmuch as he had 
been separated from the service for more than one year was not eligible for reinstate￾ment under the rules. The Secretary of War in recommending the issuance of this 
order stated that the position of interpreter for the Apache Indians at Fort Sill, Okla., 
had been vacant since Mr. Wrattan’s resignation, and that the necessity for the em￾ployment of an interpreter was very urgent, that his qualifications for the position 
were well known, and that there was probably not another white man in the United 
States who could speak the Apache language as well as he and who was so skilled and 
experienced in managing Indians. The Commission regarded the case as one in 
which an examination could not be expected to obtain the results usually obtained 
by examinations and concurred in the recommendation for the issuance of the above 
order. 
June 15, 1909.

130 THIRTIETH REPORT OF THE U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
August 6, 1913. 
Mr. Thomas H. Vanderford may be reinstated to an appropriate position in the Internal Revenue Service without reference to the period of his separation from the service. 
Mr. Vanderford was a deputy collector of internal revenue from October 11, 1893, to July 10, 1898, when he was removed for political reasons. A former collector of internal revenue, under whom he served and by whom he was separated from the service, makes the following statement regarding him in a letter dated May 9, 1913: “Mr. Vanderford was an officer in the service when I was appointed collector in 
1898 and had been for four years prior to my appointment. He served under me for practically a year. I regarded him as one of the best officers in the service and after 10 years’ experience as collector I think I can truthfully say he was as good an officer as I ever knew. I separated him from the service in order to appoint a man of my own party.” The Commissioner of Internal Revenue in a letter dated July 7, 1913, states that he has personally “known Mr. Vanderford for many years, that he is a man of sterling integrity, honest and fearless, and in his opinion possesses just such traits of character as would make a competent and efficient revenue officer. The records of the Internal Bevoune Bureau show that he rendered satisfactory service and was an efficient employee. 
In view of the above facts the commission concurs with the recommendation of the Sag of the Treasury and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue for the issuance of this order. 
August 9, 1913. 
Miss Sarah A. Prender, who is now serving as a skilled laborer in the Post Office Department, may be appointed to a clerical position not higher than class E on the permanent roll of that department without regard to the civil-service act. 
August 20, 1913. 
Mr. Charles M. McCabe may be reinstated as a clerk in the Postal Service without reference to the year limitation of the reinstatement rule. Mr. McCabe was removed from the Nashville, Tenn., post, office on September 10, 1898, notice of his removal alleging ‘‘inefficiency.”” No charge of inefficiency had been preferred against him and he was allowed no opportunity to reply to the charge as required by the rules then in effect. Mr. McCabe as a member of the board of civil service examiners for the Nashville post office rendered assistance to the commission in connection with investigations involving the collector of internal revenue, who was removed by the President for violation of the civil service rules. The Postmaster General states that it appears that Mr. McCabe was removed on political grounds, and the issuance of an Executive order for his reinstaterient seems to be justified by the facts in the case. In view of the facts stated above the Civil Service Commission concurs in recom- mending this order. 
August 25, 1913. 
Section 3 of the Regulations Governing Appointments to the Navy-Yard Service is hereby waived so as to permit of the appointment of Pedro Abrain to the position of 
general helper at $2.32 per diem at the navy yard, Mare Island, Cal. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy and is based upon the fact that Abrain was injured in the line of duty as a fireman on board the U. S. 8. Prometheus and is unable to perform the duties of a fireman. 
August 25, 1913. 
Section 3 of the Regulations Governing Appointments to the Navy-Yard Service is hereby waived so as to permit of the Sppeinishens of Edmond Pawellik to the position 
of general helper at $1.76 per diem at the navy yard, Norfolk, Va. This order 1s issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy and is based upon the fact that Pawellik was discharged from the Navy owing to injuries received in the line of duty and is unable to obtain civil employment. 
September 4, 1913. 
Mr. Pat O'Keefe may be appointed a deputy collector of internal revenue without examination under the civil-service rules. The commission was not consulted regarding this appointment. The reasons stated for the order are that Mr. O’ Keefe possesses excellent qualifications for work of this character, particularly in view of the income-tax provisions of the new tariff bill, and it was desirable that the collector of internal revenue for the State of Texas, where Mr. 0’ Keefe resides, should hava on his staff a man of Mr, O’ Keefe’s peculiar qualifications,

September 11, 1913. 
Mr. James D. Scott may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service, without regard to the length of time he has been out of the service. The Postmaster General reports that he was appointed a railway mail clerk on October 17, 1900, at $800 per annum, and promoted through the successive grades until he received a salary of $1,100 per annum; that he resigned voluntarily, April 17,1911; that his record as a clerk is good, and his reinstatement would be to the benefit of the service. Miss Emily W. Matter, of the District of Columbia, now temporarily employed in

September 17, 1913. 
Mrs. Annie S. Renick, of the District of Columbia, may be appointed to the position of clerk at $1,000 per annum in the Department of State, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. 
September 18, 1913. 
Mr. William B. Green may be reinstated as a compositor in the Weather Bureau without reference to the time limit imposed by the civil-service rules. 
Mr. Green’s services as a compositor were terminated on December 31, 1910, after more than 20 years’ service. The reason given at the time was that a reduction of the force was necessary because of the transfer of certain work from the Weather Bureau to the Government Printing Office. The Secretary of Agriculture with the concur- rence of the Civil Service Commission recommends the reinstatement because there is reason to believe that Mr. Green was unfairly dealt with because of certain testimony he had given in a case which resulted in the reprimand of the Chief of the Weather Bureau. 
September 18, 1913. 
Mr. David A. Robbins, formerly a letter carrier at Boston, Mass., may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Postal Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service.

making the removal. The right of removal, therefore, remains as it has always
been—discretionary on the part of the appointing officer, the only limitations being
that it must be to promote the efficiency of the service; that it must not be for
political or religious considerations, and that nothing shall be done in the dark; that
the reasons shall be stated and notice given to the person removed, who shall have
his opportunity to make answer and to place on file his side of the case. In order
that he may do this the reasons must be stated with sufficient definiteness to enable
him to understand the exact cause for which his removal is sought and to make an
appropriate answer. A mere general statement of inefficiency, misconduct, negli¬
gence, inattention to duty, etc., would not be sufficient. It is believed that the con¬
struction promulgated on May 29, 1902, has been in the interest of good administra¬
tion, and no case of the removal of any person from the public service for improper
reasons has since been brought to the attention of the Commission. The Commission,
on the contrary, believes that even under the present construction a far greater
number of employees who ought to be removed will be retained in the service than
the number of removals of those who ought to be retained. Appointing officers are
usually very reluctant to make removals which involve hardship upon the persons
removed.
June 2, 1902.
The following special rule was promulgated:
SPECIAL RULE.
An appointment to the vacancy now existing in the position of assistant commis¬
sioner of immigration at the port of New York may be made without examination
under the civil-service rules.
It was believed that at the port of New York the position of assistant commissioner
of immigration involved the exercise of administrative functions of a character
which could not be well provided by competitive examination, and the condition of
the immigration office at the time this rule was made was believed to be such that
the discretion of the President should not be limited in regard to the appointment
of the assistant commissioner.
June 21, 1902.
The following special rule was promulgated:
SPECIAL RULE.
The vacancy now existing in the position of clerk of class 4, for designation as
disbursing clerk in the Department of Justice, may be filled by the transfer of Mr.
Alexander C. Caine from the excepted position of examiner which he now holds in
the same Department.
The reason for this rule was the belief of the Department of Justice that the
financial responsibility involved in this place was such as to require a larger latitude
in making the selection than was permitted by the transfer rule.
June 28, 1902.
Section 1 of Pule Y was amended by adding thereto the following as a proviso:
Provided, That in order to secure a sufficient number of eligibles to meet the needs
of the service, foreign-born persons who have declared their intention to become
citizens of the United States may be admitted to examinations for the position of
copperplate map engraver.
Notwithstanding repeated efforts, the Commission had failed to secure a sufficient
number of qualified persons for the position of copperplate map engraver who were
citizens of the United States. It was understood, however, that while in this coun¬
try this work is practically confined to the Government bureaus, in England, Scot¬
land, and Germany there are a number of private establishments in which it is done
and from which qualified persons might be obtained. For these reasons and on
account of the necessities of the case the above amendment was recommended.

March 6, 1902.
Albert H. Clark had been a laborer in the office of the Chief of Engineers, War
Department, on the regular rolls since March 16, 1898. His work had been mostly
as an assistant in the copperplate printing of maps; and, on account of his ability,
experience, and knowledge of the general work of the office, he was particularly fitted
for the position of assistant messenger. On February 17, 1902, a letter was received
from the Engineer Corps, indicating that Mr. Clark, in the performance of work to
which he had been assigned, had ruptured himself in such a manner that he was not
able to do the heavy work required in the position he then occupied, and that it was
the desire of the Department to promote him to a position for which he was better
qualified physically.
Mr. Clark had been examined for the position of messenger on October 1, 1901,
and passed with a grade of 85.80, and was on the register for the State of New York,
there being at this time about 35 persons, not including preference claimants, ahead
of him. The State of New York, under the apportionment, was entitled to 726
appointments, and had received 83-f per cent.
In view of the fact that Mr. Clark was injured in the performance of the duties
assigned to him in the service of the Government, the Commission believed his case
to be a meritorious one, deserving of special action on the part of the Executive,
and recommended that it be authorized to issue a certificate for his original appoint¬
ment to the position for which the requisition of February 10, 1902, was made.
This recommendation received the President’s approval March 6, 1902.

June 15, 1898.
AMENDMENT TO RULE VIII.
Rule VIII is hereby amended by inserting after section 5 the following as section
6, and by renumbering accordingly the section now numbered 6 and succeeding
sections:
6. Certifications for appointment to clerical positions and to positions in any of the
recognized trades in the Government. Printing Office shall be so made as to maintain,
as nearly as the conditions of good administration will warrant, the apportionment
of such appointments among the several States and Territories and the District of
Columbia upon the basis of population, according to the number of employees pro¬
vided by law for that office who are affected by the provisions of this section.
Approved.
William McKinley.
Executive Mansion, June 15, 1898.
January 20, 1899.
SPECIAL RULE.a
Persons appointed temporarily under the provisions of Rule VIII, clause 12, of
the civil-service rules, in the Navy Department, may be treated as absolutely in the
classified civil service under the following conditions:
1. That such persons entered on duty prior to September 15, 1898, and have been
continuously in the service.
2. That the services of such persons have proved satisfactory to their immediate
superiors, who shall certify that they can not be dispensed with without detriment
to the public interests.
3. That such persons shall have attained an efficiency record of 75 for the six
months ended December 31, 1898, under the provisions of Navy Departmental Order
No. 13, adopted by the Commission July 29, 1896.
4. Such persons shall not be eligible for transfer to positions in the Departments
at Washington except after service of six months and under the conditions prescribed
in Civil-Service Rule X and upon a statement by the head of the department request¬
ing the transfer that the conditions of good administration demand the appointment
of the person nominated because of some special requirement of the place or qualifi¬
cations of the person for the place which can not otherwise be reasonably met.
Every absolute appointment under this rule shall be reported to the Civil Service
Commission in the usual monthly reports of the department.
Approved January 20, 1899.
William McKinley.

REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 115 
time which has elapsed since her eligibility for reinstatement expired and because of her good record of efficiency while in the service, the Civil Service Commission believes that her reinstatement is in the interests of good administration and joins the department in recommending the approval of an Executive order permitting her reinstatement. 
December 12, 1910. 
Mr. Charles M. Irelan may be reinstated as a clerk at $900 per annum in the office of the Chief of Engineers, War Department, notwithstanding the fact that somewhat more than a year elapsed between the date of his separation and the date of request for a certificate for his reinstatement. : 
The commission joins with the department in this recommendation, in view of the unusual service and exceptional efficiency of Mr. Irelan for more than 30 years in the Patent Office, and in view of the fact that he would have been reinstated in the office of the Chief of Engineers within the year of his eligibility if a suitable clerical vacancy had occurred. 
December 16, 1910. 
Mr. Edward K. Ketchum may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Philadelphia, Pa., post office, without reference to the year limitation of the civil-service rules. This order is issued in view of injuries received by Mr. Ketchum while serving as a letter carrier and engaged in making collections of mail which resulted in serious disability, compelling him to be absent from duty frequently to such an extent that on January 14, 1904, he was compelled to resign. For this reason and in view of Mr. Ketchum’s good character, his record for faithfulness and efficiency, and the fact that he is now physically able to perform the duties of a letter carrier as testified to by the Postmaster General, and as he is not entitled to compensation under the act of May 30, 1908, granting to certain employees of the United States the right to receive from the Government compensation for injuries sustained in the course of their employ- ment, the Civil Service Commission joined with the Postmaster General in recom- mending waiver of the one-year limitation of the reinstatement rule in the interests of the service. 
January 4, 1911. 
Mrs. Florence G. Miller, widow of the late Lieut. Edward Y. Miller, United States Army, may be appointed a clerk in the classified service of the United States, subject to such tests of fitness as the Civil Service Commission may require. 
Notable in achievement, the exceptionally arduous and efficient service of Lieut. Miller is entitled to special consideration. He was detailed in 1902 to civil duty in the isolated Province of Palawan, Philippine Islands, a province inhabited princi- pally by uncivilized peoples, and during this entire service of eight years his devoted wife shared his lot. He was drowned in the performance of his official duty. This service was characterized by the Chief of Staff before the military committee of the House of Representatives as more than equal through its personal influence to a battalion of troops, and was recently made the subject of a formal resolution of the Philippine civil commission, recognizing the splendid work which he did and the vicissitudes which he and his wife endured in their exile for an unbroken period of eight years as meriting the substantial recognition of Congress. Mrs. Miller is left without sufficient means for the support of herself and child. While this case is so extraordinary and exceptional as to place it in a class by itself and amply to justify special recognition, the appointment of Mrs. Miller, who is known to be a woman of high character and attainments, subject to demonstration of her qualifications by the usual civil-service examination, appears to be meritorious and in the interests of the public service. The Civil Service Commission joins the Secre- tary of War in recommending the issuance of this order. 
January 26, 1911. 
Mr. George T. Weitzel, of Missouri, a graduate of Harvard University and of the Harvard Law School, may be appointed without examination as a clerk in the Depart- ment of State because of his services as secretary of the legation to Nicaragua and Costa Rica, as secretary of legation at Panama, and in the Division of Latin-American Affairs of the Department of State. : Mr. Willing Spencer, of Pennsylvania, a graduate of Harvard University and of the University of Pennsylvania Law School, may be appointed without examination 
as a clerk in the Department of State because of his services as third secretary of embassy in St. Petersburg. The gentlemen were appointed to the Diplomatic Service through examination, 
and their appointments to competitive classified positions in the Department of State

are recommended by the Secretary of State with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission because of the experience which they have obtained while serving in diplomatic positions, which experience could not be obtained elsewhere or through open competitive examination. 
January 30, 1911. 
Mrs. Edith F. Spofford may be appointed from the Library of Congress, the em- ployees of which are not classified, to a clerical position in the Bureau of Mines, to take charge of the library of that bureau. Mrs. Spofford has had 12 years’ experience in the work of the Library of Con- gress which is regarded as a training school for cataloguers and is at present in charge of the catalogue and periodical division in that library. The relations of the Library of Congress to the Bureau of Mines as a means of obtaining indexed and catalogued data are such as to make it especially desirable that an expert trained and experienced in the work of the Library of Congress shall be employed. Through the library of which Mrs. Spofford will be in charge all purchases for the larger technical library located in the Pittsburg office of the Bureau of Mines will be made and the books, periodicals, etc., catalogued. Mrs. Spofford is said to be familiar with German in addition to being an experienced cataloguer and to have a working knowledge of several other languages and is considered by the Librarian of Congress and the heads of divisions in which she has been employed as qualified for the position. The Civil Service Commission joined with the Secretary of the Interior in recommending this Executive order in the interests of good administration in view of the facts. 
January 30, 1911. 
Mr. Archibald Edmonstone was removed from the position of weigher in the Customs Service at New York on May 11, 1909, with three other weighers, who were believed to be responsible for much of the corruption in their division. It appears from the statements of the collector, of the Chief of the Appointment Division of the Treasury Department, and of Mr. Henry L. Stimson, who investigated the frauds, that the evidence not only failed to connect Mr. Edmonstone with the frauds but that the testimony of all of the witnesses who were examined was unanimous in stating that he never participated in the frauds. may allow transfer to any other Department or office upon his passing an exam¬
ination prescribed by the Commission testing his efficiency for the position to
which his transfer is proposed, subject to the other provisions of this rule.
The effect of this amendment to the rules was to provide that the Commission
might waive the requirement of six months’ service preceding transfer in meri¬
torious eases. The reason for this was that in a large number of cases persons
had been separated from the Government Printing Office and from the Bureau
of Pensions through no fault of their own, but because of the necessary reduc¬
tion of force. There was a need for such employees in some of the other De¬
partments, but because they had already been separated from the service they
could not be transferred under the old rule until they had been reinstated and
served a period of six months after reinstatement.
NONCOMPETITIVE EXAMINATIONS FOR INDIANS.

Section 2 of Rule III is hereby amended by adding after the words “ indus¬
trial teachers ” the words “ and in the Office of Indian Affairs in the messenger
service.”
As amended the section will read:
2. Where, in its opinion, the conditions of good administration warrant, the
Commission may give rioncompetitive examinations to test fitness for (a) trans¬
fer, reinstatement, or promotion; (b) appointment of Indians in the Indian
service at large as superintendents, teachers, manual-training teachers, kinder￾gartners, physicians, matrons, clerks, seamstresses, farmers, and industrial
teachers, and in the Office of Indian Affairs in the messenger service, which ex¬
aminations shall consist of the same tests of fitness as those applied to other

Trior to this order the rules provided for the appointment of Indians on non¬
competitive examination in certain positions in the Indian field service, but

CERTIFICATION.

Rule VII, in regard to certification, was entirely rewritten under date of
January 27, 1908. The changes embodied in this order were the provision to

sufficient eligibles to fill several vacancies when a requisition for a number of

groups of three; and the provision that an eligible who had been three times

mission, if the condition of the register had not changed so as to place him in

VIII in regard to temporary appointments. The rule governing temporary ap¬
pointments was entirely rewritten at the time of its amendment. The principal

change w£is iir regard to temporary appointments pending the filling of a perma¬
nent position. Under the old rule the Department had general authority by
the terms of the rule to make such appointments for a period not to exceed
thirty days. Under the rule as amended the prior authority of the Commission
must be secured in each case for such appointments. General authority has
been given by the Commission for appointments of this kind for various periods

been somewhat relieved of the importunities of the applicants for temporary

Marshall” to the position of postmaster at Elko, Ga. The commission is further advised that the post-office inspector who was sent by the department to investigate and make recommendation for an appointment, recom- mended eligible John H. Clark, and that Mr. Marshall’s name be placed second ,on the list. The inspector’s report shows that Marshall had been in charge of the office for some months; that he was assistant postmaster prior to the death of the late post- master, that his services were satisfactory to the public, and that he was capable and painstaking, and was Dopaler in the community. : fae appointment of Mr. Marshall will be treated as an appointment by Executive 
order. 
December 14, 1912. 
Miss Alice Engle may be appointed to a clerical position in the Department of Agri- culture without regard to the civil-service rules. Miss Engle’s name is on the West Virginia typewriter register with a rating of 81.65 but not within reach for certification for probational appointment. She was selected for temporary appointment from this register. The Secretary of Agriculture recommends the issuance of this order, but the Civil Service Commission does not concur. 
December 16, 1912. 
On the 28th day of October, 1912, the President issued an Executive order author- izing the appointment of Mr. Guy Emerson as a special agent of the Treasury Depart￾ment without compliance with the civil-service rules, for the reasons therein stated. Since that time conditions have arisen which make it advisable for the Secretary of the Treasury to have a broader discretion in the matter of Mr. Emerson’s appointment 
in the interest of a better accomplishment of the purposes had in view in that order than the order gives him. The order is therefore hereby amended so as to authorize the Secretary of the Treasury to appoint Mr. Guy Emerson, without compliance with the civil-service rules, to any competitive classified position in the Treasury service which may be available for the purpose, and to transfer him as the interest of the service may require. 
December 17, 1912. 
Mr. Charles R. Pickard may be appointed to an appropriate position in the com￾petitive classified service without compliance with the provisions of the civil-service rules. « This action is taken because of the long and varied experience of Mr. Pickard in the 
judicial service and in the executive service in positions not subject to the civil- service rules, in all of which positions he has served efficiently and well. The Sec- retary of Commerce and Labor, under whom Mr. Pickard is temporarily employed as a special agent in the Bureau of the Census, also expresses the opinion that his appoint- ment to a competitive position will be in the interests of the Government. The Civil Service Commission is unable to recommend the issuance of this order. 
December 19, 1912. 
Mr. William C. Boutelle may be reinstated in an appropriate position in or under the Post Office Department without regard to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Boutelle was appointed on July 16, 1890, as a post-office inspector by transfer from the Railway Mail Service, where he had served for many years, and was sep- arated from the position of post-office inspector on May 16, 1893. After several years he was appointed a clerk in the post-office at Hilo, Hawaii, neither the office nor the position being classified. In 1901 he was appointed a temporary clerk in the office of the post-office inspector in charge at Honolulu, with the approval of the commission, and continued to serve under temporary appointment with the approval of the com- mission. until examinations were held in Hawaii. His temporary appointment should have ceased upon the establishment of eligibl2 registers in Hawaii, but through inadvertence of the commission and the department he was allowed to continue in the service in Hawaii, and later in the office of the post-office inspector in charge at San Francisco, Cal., until July 11, 1911. In view of his long service and the apparent irregular administration of both the commission and the department in the Hawaiian Islands during the years of his tem- porary service, the commission recommends his classification by Executive order.

December 19, 1912. 
Mr. Horace P. DeHart may be transferred from the excepted position of confidential 
clerk to the Assistant Secretary of the Interior to an appropriate competitive position in that department. Mr. DeHart has served continuously as confidential clerk for more than nine years to four assistant secretaries. During that period he has acquired a comprehensive knowledge of the varied business assigned to the assistant secretary, which includes numerous Indian matters, including contracts and bonds, leases, heirship cases, petitions for the approval of sale, etc., appeals in land cases, pension appeals, business 
relating to .eleemosynary institutions, expense and transportation accounts, and many miscellaneous items. His practical experience has made him a useful, efficient and well-trained clerk, and according to the Secretary of the Interior his retention in the service will contribute effectively to the despatch of important business. In view of the proved capacity and exceptional qualifications of Mr. DeHart, the Civil Service Commission joins in the recommendation for his transfer to a competitive position by Executive order. 
December 19, 1912. 
Mr. Thomas E. Price may be promoted from the position of messenger to that of clerk in the Post Office Department without examination. The Postmaster General states that for more than 10 years Mr. Price has been engaged in opening letters in the Division of Dead Letters, and the incessant use of his right Eos has resulted in partial paralysis. He recommends this order, believing that a change in duties will prevent permanent injury. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
December 30, 1912. 
Mr. Samuel E. Fouts may be reinstated as an assistant examiner in the Patent Office, Department of the Interior, without reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Fouts was appointed an assistant examiner through examination on April 6, 1894, and resigned on.September 11, 1899. Since that date he has been actively engaged in the practice of patent law. He attained a high rank as an examiner of ability and efficiency in the Patent Office, and his experience since his separation has given him unusual qualifications for resuming his Patent Office work. REGULATIONS GOVERNING THE APPOINTMENT OF RURAL CARRIERS. 
[Approved Feb. 19, 1912.] 
The following regulations govern appointment to the position of carrier in the 
Rural Delivery Service: 
1. Examinations shall be held only as the needs of the service require; where 
the department orders the establishment of a route embracing territory not 
previously supplied by rural delivery service a new examination shall be held. 
An examination shall be held for each. county in which eligibles are needed. 
A person must be examined in the county in which the post office that supplies 
his home is situated. As a result of such examination he may become eligible 
to appointment as rural carrier at any post office in such county. Examinations 
will be held by local examining boards or other representatives of the commis￾sion. In counties where no local examining board has been organized a post￾master or other official of the Government may be called upon to act as an 
examiner. 
As men are desired for appointment to this service, women will not be ad￾mitted to the examination. 
2. The commission may refuse to examine an applicant— 
(a) Who is not a citizen of or does not owe allegiance to the United States. 
(b) Who is not actually domiciled within the territory supplied by a post 
office situated in the county for which the examination is held; that is to say, 
the county for which a person may be examined is the county in which the 
post office that supplies his home is situated. 
(¢) Who is on the date of the examination under 18 years of age or over 50 
years of age. The maximum age limit is waived in cases of persons honorably 
discharged from the United States military or naval service. 
(d) Who has any of the following defects: Insanity, tuberculosis, paralysis, 
epilepsy, loss of arm or leg, loss of hand; badly crippled or deformed hands, 
arms, feet, or legs; uncompensated valvular disease of the heart, locomotor 
ataxia, cancer, Bright's disease, diabetes, hunchback ; seriously defective hear￾ing, sight, or speech; asthma, hernia, or any other defect which would dis￾qualify him for the service. 
(e) Who is addicted to the habitual use of intoxicating beverages to excess. 
(f) Who has within approximately one year passed a rural-carrier examina￾tion.
